sections.title: Must: formal rules, warnings, reminders, arrangements
sections.content:
We use must and must not in formal rules and regulations and in warnings:
• Bookings must be made at least seven days before departure.
• The government must not be allowed to appoint judges.
In spoken English we often use must and mustn't (= must not) to propose a future arrangement, such as a meeting or social event, without making detailed plans:
• We must get together more often.
• We mustn't leave it so long next time.
We can also use I must … to remind ourselves to do something:
• I must charge my phone. I meant to do it yesterday, but I forgot.

sections.title: Must for strong conclusions about past, present and future
sections.content:
To draw a strong conclusion about –
☆ something that happened in the past, we use must + have + past participle:
• That's not Clara's car. She must have borrowed it from her parents.
☆ something happening at or around the time of speaking, we use must be + -ing:
• I can't hear a noise. You must be imagining things.
☆ something that is likely to happen in the future, we use must be going to or must be + -ing:
• 'What are all those workmen doing?' 'I think they must be going to dig up the road.'
• I was wrong about the meeting today. It must be happening next Friday.
☆ a present situation, we use must be, or have (got) to be in informal speech:
• Their goalkeeper has got to be at least two metres tall! (or … must be …)
We can use must have to to draw a conclusion based on what we know about a present situation and must have had to to draw a conclusion about a past situation:
• I can't access the database. You must have to put in a password. (= a password is necessary)
• Matt wasn't at home when I went round. He must have had to go out unexpectedly.
Note that we can't say 'must've (got) to' but we can say must've had to.

sections.title: Have (got) to in questions; must for criticism
sections.content:
In questions that hope for or expect a negative answer we prefer have (got) to, although in formal contexts must is sometimes used:
• Do we have to answer all the questions? (or Have we got to …?; formally Must we …?)
We use have to in questions that imply a criticism. Must can also be used, although some people think this is rather old-fashioned. We usually stress have and must in sentences like this:
• Do you have to play your trumpet here? It's deafening! (formally Must you play …?)

sections.title: Have to vs have got to: differences
sections.content:
Sometimes we can use either have to or have got to. However –
☆ we use have to with frequency adverbs (see Unit 75B):
• I often have to work at the weekend to get everything done.
☆ with the past simple we use have to, especially in questions and negative sentences:
• When did you have to give it back? (not When had you got to give it back?)
• We didn't have to wait too long for an answer. (not We hadn't got to wait too long …)
☆ if have is contracted (e.g. I've, He's, It'd) then we must include got:
• I need a new pair of shoes, and they've got to be blue. (not … they've to be …)
☆ we don't use have got to with other modal verbs:
• Motorists will have to wait until next year to use the bridge. (not Motorists will have got to wait …)
Note also that have got to is often preferred in informal speech.

exercises.question: When I left my laptop on the train... someone ___ it and handed it in. (find)
exercises.hint: Conclusion about something that happened in the past → must have + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must have found
Conclusion about something that happened in the past → must have + past participle.

exercises.question: Luisa owns a big car and a yacht. She ___ incredibly rich. (be)
exercises.hint: Conclusion about current state → must be.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must be
'Must be' expresses a logical deduction about the present based on available evidence. When you see something and draw a conclusion, 'must be' conveys the certainty of your inference.

exercises.question: Everyone's going into the hall. The meeting ___ soon.
exercises.hint: Conclusion about something happening now/very soon → must be + -ing.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must be starting
Conclusion about something happening now/very soon → must be + -ing. This verb pattern requires a gerund (-ing form) as its object.

exercises.question: Without washing machines, our grandparents ___ much harder in the kitchen.
exercises.hint: Conclusion about past necessity → must have had to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must have had to work
Conclusion about past necessity → must have had to + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: I didn't think Rob was coming. He ___ his mind.
exercises.hint: Past conclusion → must have + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must have changed
Past conclusion → must have + past participle. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: I wonder how you get past security. I suppose you ___ some form of ID.
exercises.hint: Conclusion about a present necessity/rule → must have to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must have to show
Conclusion about a present necessity/rule → must have to + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: I thought Paul would be home. He ___ Lotta to work.
exercises.hint: Past conclusion → must have + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must have taken
Past conclusion → must have + past participle. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Look at all those birds. There ___ at least a thousand of them. (be)
exercises.hint: Present conclusion about quantity → must be.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must be
'Must be' followed by a number expresses a confident estimate or logical deduction. You're reasoning from the evidence — a large number of birds — to a conclusion about quantity.

exercises.question: It is necessary to do all of this photocopying before lunchtime.
options: All of this photocopying has got to be done / has to be done before lunchtime.
All of this photocopying has got to do before lunchtime.
All of this photocopying must done before lunchtime.
All of this photocopying needs done before lunchtime.
exercises.hint: Contracted form ('this photocopying') → has got to / has to both work here.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: All of this photocopying has got to be done / has to be done before lunchtime.
Contracted form ('this photocopying') → has got to / has to both work here. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: It is rarely necessary to ask Hannah to tidy her room.
options: Hannah rarely has to be asked to tidy her room.
Hannah rarely has got to be asked to tidy her room.
Hannah rarely must be asked to tidy her room.
Hannah needn't be asked to tidy her room.
exercises.hint: Frequency adverb 'rarely' → use have to (not have got to).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Hannah rarely has to be asked to tidy her room.
Frequency adverb 'rarely' → use have to (not have got to).

exercises.question: Is it necessary for us to hand in the homework tomorrow?
exercises.answer: Have we got to hand in the homework tomorrow?
acceptable: Do we have to hand in the homework tomorrow?
Both 'Have we got to' and 'Do we have to' are correct
exercises.hint: Question about necessity — both 'have got to' and 'have to' work for questions.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both 'Have we got to' and 'Do we have to' are correct
Question about necessity — both 'have got to' and 'have to' work for questions.

exercises.question: It wasn't necessary for me to go to the hospital after all.
options: I didn't have to go to the hospital after all.
I hadn't got to go to the hospital after all.
I mustn't go to the hospital after all.
I needn't go to the hospital after all.
exercises.hint: Past negative → use 'didn't have to' (not 'hadn't got to').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I didn't have to go to the hospital after all.
Didn't have to means there was no external obligation — you were free to choose. Compare: mustn't (= you must not do it) vs didn't have to (= it wasn't required). Past negative → use 'didn't have to' (not 'hadn't got to').

exercises.question: Was it necessary for Ben to go alone?
options: Did Ben have to go alone?
Had Ben got to go alone?
Did Ben need to go alone?
exercises.hint: Past question → 'did ... have to' (not 'had... got to').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Did Ben have to go alone?
Past question → 'did ... have to' (not 'had... got to').

exercises.question: It is sometimes necessary for Adam to start work at 6:30.
options: Adam sometimes has to start work at 6:30.
Adam sometimes has got to start work at 6:30.
Adam must sometimes start work at 6:30.
Adam needs to sometimes start work at 6:30.
exercises.hint: Frequency adverb 'sometimes' → use 'have to' (not 'have got to').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Adam sometimes has to start work at 6:30.
Frequency adverb 'sometimes' → use 'have to' (not 'have got to').

exercises.question: Email: '...I (2) always have got to pull it very hard to shut it.' What is the correction?
options: always have to pull (frequency adverb → 'have to' not 'have got to')
exercises.hint: With frequency adverb 'always' → use 'have to' not 'have got to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: always have to pull (frequency adverb → 'have to' not 'have got to')
With frequency adverb 'always' → use 'have to' not 'have got to'. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Email: '(3) Have you to bang the door so hard?' What is the correction?
options: Do you have to bang (correct question form)
exercises.hint: Correct question form for have to → 'Do you have to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Do you have to bang (correct question form)
Correct question form for have to → 'Do you have to'.

exercises.question: Email: 'someone (5) must have to squeeze through the tiny window.' What is the correction?
options: must have had to squeeze (past necessity conclusion)
exercises.hint: Conclusion about past necessity → must have had to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must have had to squeeze (past necessity conclusion)
Conclusion about past necessity → must have had to.

exercises.question: Email: 'I (8) mustn't wait very long for the police to get here.' What is the correction?
options: didn't have to wait (past, it wasn't necessary)
exercises.hint: It was not necessary (and they came quickly) → didn't have to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: didn't have to wait (past, it wasn't necessary)
Didn't have to means there was no external obligation — you were free to choose. Compare: mustn't (= you must not do it) vs didn't have to (= it wasn't required). It was not necessary (and they came quickly) → didn't have to.

exercises.question: Email: 'the burglars (9) must be disturbed.' What is the correction?
options: must have been disturbed (past passive conclusion)
exercises.hint: Past conclusion, passive → must have been disturbed.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must have been disturbed (past passive conclusion)
Past conclusion, passive → must have been disturbed. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Email: '(10) I've to get a new lock.' What is the correction?
options: I've got to get (contracted have → must use 'got to')
exercises.hint: When 'have' is contracted ('I've'), must include 'got' → I've got to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I've got to get (contracted have → must use 'got to')
When 'have' is contracted ('I've'), must include 'got' → I've got to.

exercises.sentence: You must to finish the report before five o'clock.
exercises.correction: You must finish the report before five o'clock.
acceptable: You must finish the report before five o'clock.
You have to finish the report before five o'clock.
exercises.hint: 'Must' is followed by the bare infinitive — no 'to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: You must finish
'Must' is a modal verb and is always followed by the bare infinitive (no 'to'). 'Must to finish' is a very common learner error — possibly influenced by 'have to', which does use 'to'.

exercises.sentence: He musted leave early because of a family emergency.
exercises.correction: He had to leave early because of a family emergency.
exercises.hint: 'Must' has no past tense form — use 'had to' for past obligation.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: He had to leave early
'Must' has no past form. To express past obligation or necessity, use 'had to + infinitive'. This applies in all past tense contexts: 'We had to wait', 'She had to cancel', 'They had to apologise'.

exercises.sentence: The windows must be cleaning every week.
exercises.correction: The windows must be cleaned every week.
acceptable: The windows must be cleaned every week.
The windows have to be cleaned every week.
exercises.hint: Passive obligation: must + be + past participle (not -ing).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must be cleaned
The passive form after 'must' is: must + be + past participle. 'Must be cleaning' would mean an ongoing action is obligatory right now — but here we want a general rule (every week), so the infinitive passive is correct.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the correct order:
exercises.hint: Subject + had to + bare infinitive + adverb (past obligation)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She had to leave early
'Must' has no past form. To express past obligation, use 'had to + bare infinitive'. The structure: subject (she) + had to (past obligation) + leave (bare infinitive) + early (adverb). Compare: 'She must leave early' (present) → 'She had to leave early' (past).
